title: Prompt Engineering and AI Red Teaming — Sander Schulhoff, HackAPrompt/LearnPrompting
talk_summary: Sander Schulhoff surveys prompt-engineering research (the Prompt Report) and AI red teaming, arguing that most prompt tricks are weakly validated, that automated prompt optimization (DSPy) beat 20 hours of manual prompt engineering, and that prompt injection/jailbreaks are fundamentally unsolvable so agents must be sandboxed and treated as untrusted.

takeaways.technique: Automated prompt optimization beats manual prompt tuning
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of hand-iterating prompts for 20 hours, they ran DSPy (automated prompt engineering) on the same task and compared F1 scores against manual attempts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: human me uh was a poor performer. The AI automated prompt engineer was a great performer. Uh and the automated prompt engineer plus human was a fantastic performer.
takeaways.numbers: Manual prompt engineering plateaued after ~10 hours; DSPy beat the best manual F1, and DSPy + light human tuning beat it further

takeaways.technique: Few-shot + chain-of-thought as the default strong baseline
takeaways.what_they_do: Benchmarked many prompting techniques on MMLU and found few-shot examples combined with chain-of-thought were the best general performers; other exotic techniques added little.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we saw that fshot uh and chain of thought uh combined uh were basically the the best uh techniques
takeaways.numbers: Best on MMLU vs ~200 catalogued techniques tested

takeaways.technique: Role prompting is useless for accuracy tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: Ran a case study giving models 'genius math professor' vs 'idiot who can't do math' roles on GSM8K; the dumb role scored higher, showing role prompts don't improve accuracy.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the dumb idiot role beat the intelligent math professor role
takeaways.numbers: Dumb role outperformed expert role across ~1-2k GSM8K questions

takeaways.technique: Prompt-level defenses and guardrails don't stop injection; sandbox instead
takeaways.what_they_do: From the HackAPrompt competition: system-prompt defenses and guardrail models were trivially bypassed (e.g. base64/translation obfuscation), while the real fix for the MathGPT incident was containerizing untrusted generated code.
takeaways.evidence_quote: There's no prompt that you can write, no system prompt that you can write that will prevent prompt injection. Just don't work.
takeaways.numbers: 40% of prompts that jailbroke GPT-3 also worked on GPT-4

takeaways.technique: Prompt transfer across models is unreliable — re-validate per model
takeaways.what_they_do: Tested successful attack prompts across models and found only partial transfer; also noted no good way to make one prompt work identically across models.
takeaways.evidence_quote: 40% of prompts that successfully attacked GPT3 also worked against GPD4

takeaways.technique: Decompose before solving; route subproblems to separate calls
takeaways.what_they_do: Least-to-most prompting asks the model what subproblems must be solved first, then sends each to separate model instances/experts and recombines answers.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it asks what are the subpros that must be solved before or in order to solve this problem uh and then solves those individually
